title: "Terms from the venue's side"
unit: 2

<Phase type="activation">

Picture a restaurant till holding the money for a banquet six months away. The restaurant needs to pay for electricity and this week's food.

**The money is right there, and it feels as if it is already yours.** Think about whose it really is.

</Phase>

<Phase type="reflection">

Go back to the till. Until the banquet happens, that money is a promise to provide a service.

**A leader's prepayment is not the venue's revenue, it is its obligation.** If a venue spends it on running costs, it is funding itself with someone else's money.

</Phase>

<Phase type="concept">

## The payment schedule

As of 2026-10, typical terms of group contracts are these:

- a first payment of 10 to 25 % of the contract at signing;
- the balance usually a week to a month before arrival;
- a point of no return 90–120 days before arrival, after which the charge rises to 100 %.

A venue builds its own schedule from its own obligations. When the kitchen buys food, when staff turn down other shifts, when the week can no longer be sold night by night.

## The minimum guarantee

The minimum is the number of guests or share of places the leader pays for in any case. In hotel contracts it is usually 70–90 % of the block. Retreat centres more often fix a number of guests a few weeks before arrival.

A minimum that is too high scares leaders off. One that is too low leaves the venue with an empty week.

## What happens when the group is short

Open the [teaching deal "a full campus, 12 came"](https://academy.synergify.com/en/instrumenty/kalkulyator-retrita/#) and switch the calculator to the venue's view. The venue gets 36,000 dollars. The leader loses 1,080 and is unlikely to come back.

Now [the same week with per-guest pricing and a minimum of 14](https://academy.synergify.com/en/instrumenty/kalkulyator-retrita/#). The venue gets 25,200, and the leader earns 9,720. The venue got less today, but it kept a leader for next year.

## Where the money is kept

There is a known case of a retreat centre that closed after a natural disaster and owed groups about 200,000 dollars in deposits. The money was not kept separately. The honest approach is not to spend leaders' prepayments on running costs and to keep them so that they can be returned.

This is not legal advice. In some countries and situations, holding prepayments is regulated by law — check with a lawyer.

<SelfCheck id="c2"/>

</Phase>

<Phase type="practice">

1. Open both teaching deals through the links above and write down what the venue and the leader get in each.
2. List your obligations for a group's week: food purchases, staff, giving up nightly lets — with dates.
3. Build your scale from them: the first payment, the point of no return, the charge steps.
4. Choose a minimum group that protects you and does not scare off a new leader.
5. Write the terms on one page: the schedule, the minimum, cancellations, where prepayments are kept.

</Phase>
